newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr dives 1/2 cent after dire sales data.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr dives 1/2 cent after dire sales data.

text.p: The Australian dollar dived over 1/2 cent at the midsession as a fledgling rally was cruelly undermined by shockingly weak retail trade data.

The currency had just managed to clear US$0.7675 resistance after a week of struggle when sales were reported to have fallen 1.7 percent in April, confounding expectations of a 0.5 percent rise. The drop came on the back of a 0.3 percent dip in March,, the first back-to-back falls since mid-1993.
The dire data not only justified last week's Reserve Bank rate cut but raised the prospect of yet another easing, so dealers looked for the dollar to test its recent US$0.7615 low.
By 12.30 pm (0230 GMT) the local dollar had crumbled to US$0.7619/24 from US$0.7680/85 just before the data hit dealing screens and US$0.7658/63 late here Thursday.
Traders said there was corporate and options-related bids around US$0.7615, the low from Wednesday, which were providing some support for the moment.

However, dealers doubted offshore investors would be keen to hold the currency with short term domestic money rates sinking further past those in the U.S. as the market contemplated another official easing. U.S. investment banks had already been aggressive sellers and they feared others would soon join in.

If US$0.7615 did snap, dealers expected a quick fall to a pivotal chart level at US$0.7550 which marks the low for the year so far reached in February. A breach there would return the currency to levels not seen since February 1996 and would be extremely bearish on a technical view.

On the crosses the currency dipped to 88.75/85 yen from 89.20/30 late Thursday but the damage was limited by a sharp fall in Japanese bond yields following weak industrial production data there. The data reassured the market the Bank of Japan would probably not be raising rates soon, even though an LDP committe had recommended the government hike in the future.
But Japanese yields were not the only ones falling, with the 3-year Commonwealth bond down 19 basis points to 6.16 percent.

The 90-day bank bill future, which best mirrors market thinking on official rates, leapt 15 basis points to 94.63 for the September contract, implying a rate of 5.37 percent against the present cash rate of 5.5 percent.
"It's amazing the difference a week makes," said one dealer, noting that before last Friday the market had been pricing in a hike by year end and the dollar was testing US$0.7860.
"Now we've had one cut and are looking down the barrel of another, and the Aussie seems destined for US$0.7550."
Supporting the soft message from the sales data was an unexpected 6.0 percent fall in motor vehicle registrations for April, formely a strong segment of consumer spending.

There was better news on baance of payments with ther current account deficit narrowing to A$4.587 billion in the March quarter from A$5.262 billion in Q4. The improvement came on the trade side where the balance of goods and services posted a A$654 million surplus and net exports promised to make a positive contribution to GDP growth in the quarter of around 0.6 percentage points.
